video_title: How a Sardine Gets From the Ocean to a Can | Odd Lots
gist: Fishwife founder/CEO Becca Millstein walks Tracy Alloway and Joe Weisenthal through the canned-seafood supply chain and the Moroccan frozen-sardine export ban that has wiped sardine shelves and pushed Fishwife's sardine velocities up 4-5x. The conversation is a case study in a hollowed-out processing base (only ~5 canneries left in the lower 48), multi-generational European canneries that grow 5% a year being asked to serve a brand growing 250%, and how a premium brand built pricing power in a category that was flat-to-declining five years ago. Secondary threads: a 15% EU tariff costing millions, MSC-certified fishery sourcing as supply insurance, and why farmed salmon wins on working capital.

insights.claim: Morocco, which reportedly supplies roughly 50% of the world's sardines, has banned sardine exports citing overfishing, removing the single largest source of raw sardine from the global market.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: A single-country export restriction on ~half of global supply is a hard supply shock for every canned-fish brand and private-label retailer; watch shelf gaps and price pass-through in canned seafood.
insights.quote: Morocco, which apparently exports something like 50% of the world's sardine supply

insights.claim: The Moroccan restriction is a ban on frozen sardine exports only, not on canned sardine exports, meaning Morocco is deliberately retaining raw material to protect the margin of its own domestic canning industry.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: This is industrial policy dressed as conservation: value-add capture moves onshore in Morocco while European canners lose input, so the shortage should show up as European processing underutilization rather than a global calorie shortage.
insights.quote: the ban is just on frozen sardine exports

insights.claim: Roughly 90% of the raw sardine material processed in Spanish canneries came from the Moroccan fishery, making Spain the single most exposed downstream economy to the export ban.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Spanish canning capacity is effectively a single-source supply chain; any brand sourcing from Spanish sardine canneries carries concentrated country risk unless it has an alternate fishery.
insights.quote: I think it was like 90% of the raw material, in Spanish canneries of sardines was coming from Morocco.

insights.claim: The Moroccan sardine catch was already down roughly 46% in 2023, three years before the export ban was imposed, showing the shortage was visible in catch data long before it hit shelves.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Catch-volume data leads consumer shortages by years; monitoring national landings statistics gives an early warning on canned-seafood cost inflation.
insights.quote: they started to see a decline in the catch in 2023. It was about it was down about 46%.

insights.claim: The sardine export ban has escalated into a diplomatic dispute, with Spain seeking to bring Morocco to the negotiating table to get the ban lifted.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: A resolution is a political event, not a biological one, so the shortage could reverse faster than fishery science would imply if Spain wins concessions.
insights.quote: the Moroccan sardine export ban is now becoming a diplomatic

insights.claim: Chinese sardine processors are running B2B Instagram ads that explicitly name the Moroccan sardine shortage as the reason to switch suppliers, showing Asian processing capacity is actively marketing into the supply gap.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Expect share of canned sardine supply to shift toward low-cost Asian processors during the ban, which pressures quality positioning and creates label-provenance risk for buyers.
insights.quote: are you dealing with the Moroccan sardine shortage?

themes.theme: Climate vs. overfishing as the real cause

insights.claim: The most likely explanation for the sardine decline is warming waters in the Mid-Atlantic driving forage fish like sardines, anchovies and mackerel to migrate to colder or deeper water rather than an outright population collapse.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: If the fish moved rather than died, the supply problem is about fleet access and geography, which can be solved with new fishing grounds far faster than a stock rebuild.

insights.claim: Warmer water can also increase the number of active predators such as tuna in a fishery, so human catch declines can reflect competition from other species rather than human overfishing.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Predation-driven declines are not fixed by quota policy, so export bans and closures may under-deliver on stock recovery.

insights.claim: The plankton theory holds that warmer water produces less nutrient-dense, leaner plankton, which in turn produces leaner and less fatty sardines that are commercially less desirable to catch.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Quality degradation, not just volume, drives the shortage: even a recovering catch may yield fish that premium canners will not buy, keeping premium prices elevated longer than headline catch data suggests.

insights.claim: Overfishing is probably not the main culprit in the Moroccan sardine situation because Monterey Bay Aquarium Seafood Watch currently gives the fishery a yellow rating and assesses it as well regulated with strong enforcement in place.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Third-party sustainability ratings are a usable independent signal for separating regulatory-driven supply cuts from genuine stock collapse when assessing seafood suppliers.

insights.claim: Fishery closures and export caps should be read as responsible fisheries management working, not as a crisis signal, because fisheries that shut down for roughly 3 to 5 years have repeatedly become certified sustainable again.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: A 3-5 year closure is a usable base rate for modeling when banned supply returns, which frames how long a shortage-driven price regime can persist.
insights.quote: don't freak out when you see when you see those empty shelves, like be happy that like people are putting these restrictions into place

insights.claim: Seafood sustainability assessments move far slower than the market reacts because fishery stock assessments take a very long time, so public explanations for a shortage remain competing theories rather than settled science.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Do not underwrite a seafood supply thesis on a single headline cause; the information lag means prices move well before the science resolves.

insights.claim: Fishwife's sardine sales began accelerating in December of last year and velocities have run 2-3x and sustained up to 4-5x prior levels, despite Fishwife never sourcing from the Moroccan fishery.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Impairment of a commodity supply chain reroutes demand into the premium tier, so branded premium players are the volume beneficiaries of a commodity shortage even with unaffected raw material.
insights.quote: December of last year, like start to go cuckoo bananas

insights.claim: Fishwife repeatedly chose to airfreight sardines to retailers with empty shelves, accepting compressed gross margin in exchange for capturing shortage demand and acquiring new customers.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Shortage-driven revenue spikes in CPG can come with a margin cost; read a competitor's or portfolio company's volume surge alongside freight mode before assuming operating leverage.
insights.quote: are we okay with our gross margin being compressed

insights.claim: Fishwife expects its sardine prices to rise as the two MSC-certified fisheries it sources from become more competitively bid, and describes it as an active internal conversation.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Watch for premium canned fish price increases as a leading indicator of raw-material competition spreading beyond Morocco into MSC-certified European fisheries.
insights.quote: I do think that we expect our, our starting prices to go up.

insights.claim: Retail buyers are directly calling brands asking them to step in and fill wiped-out sardine shelves, which is how a supply shock converts into distribution wins for a challenger brand.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Shortages are a shelf-space land grab; challenger brands that can physically deliver during a gap can lock in placement that survives the shortage.

insights.claim: Canned-fish consumers trade across species rather than exiting the category, with observed substitution between sardines, mackerel, tuna, salmon and trout, but not into anchovies because anchovies are not treated as a meal protein.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Cross-species substitution means a sardine shortage lifts demand and pricing across the whole tinned-protein set, so the trade is the category rather than the single species.

insights.claim: Food inflation drives consumers to trade up rather than down in some categories, on the logic that if ground beef costs $20 a pack you may as well spend $30 on steak.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Premiumization can be an inflation beneficiary, not a casualty, which argues against the reflexive downtrading assumption in packaged food.
insights.quote: if I'm going to have to pay $20 for a pack of ground beef, I might as well spend $30 and get some steaks

themes.theme: US cannery collapse and offshored processing

insights.claim: Nearly all US canneries shut down roughly 15 years ago, leaving an estimated five or so canneries in the lower 48 plus several more in Alaska handling commodity products like canned Alaskan salmon.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: There is effectively no domestic canning base to reshore to, so tariff or trade policy aimed at canned seafood raises costs without a viable US substitution path.
insights.quote: Basically, like all most canneries in the U.S. shut down like 15 years ago.

insights.claim: The US cannery shutdown was driven by a combination of stringent FDA rules introduced about 15 years ago that operators could not comply with, plus real declines in the Pacific sardine and anchovy fisheries that removed the raw material.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Regulatory compliance cost plus resource decline is the recurring template for how a processing industry disappears; the same pairing is worth checking in other food-processing categories.
insights.quote: there were really stringent FDA, rules or put in place about 15 years ago

insights.claim: Cheap processing capacity in China, Vietnam and Thailand absorbed the work that US canneries used to do, to the point that fish caught off Alaska is routinely shipped to China for processing before being sold in the United States.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: US-caught seafood carries embedded China exposure, so tariffs or logistics disruption on Chinese processing hit products marketed as domestic.

insights.claim: Five years ago canned fish was a flat-to-declining category in the US and industry insiders told founders to build a pouch business instead because the pouch industry was booming.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: The category's decline is precisely what left cannery slack and zero competition for line time, illustrating that dying categories can be the cheapest place to build supply-side advantage.
insights.quote: Why don't you do pouches? The pouch industry is booming.

insights.claim: The canned fish category saw roughly a 10% year-over-year increase during the Covid-19 pandemic as shelf-stable ready-to-eat protein gained share, a rate it has not repeated since.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: The Covid bump was a one-time level shift, not a durable growth rate, so category-level tailwind claims should be checked against post-2021 baselines.
insights.quote: the canvas category saw like a 10% year over year

insights.claim: Cantabrian anchovies are caught about six miles offshore in northern Spain by purse seine, iced immediately, then graded at an anchovy auction on size, damage and fattiness before cannery buyers bid, meaning quality is priced at the dock rather than negotiated on contract.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Auction-based raw material means brand input costs float daily with catch quality, so premium seafood brands cannot fully fix COGS the way a manufactured-ingredient CPG can.

insights.claim: Anchovies are salt-cured in barrels of rock salt for 12 to 36 months, with longer cures producing higher quality, so Fishwife's 12-18 month cure means raw material capital is tied up for over a year before a can can be sold.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Multi-year inventory conversion cycles make anchovy supply structurally unresponsive to demand spikes and make working capital, not marketing, the binding constraint.
insights.quote: they will be put into a barrel of rock salt in layers. And they'll be left there for anywhere between 12 to 36 months.

insights.claim: Salt-cured anchovies have only about a one-year shelf life and degrade with heat exposure, versus 5 to 7 years for Fishwife's other tinned products, making anchovies the most complex SKU to store and ship despite the simplest supply chain.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: A 5-7 year shelf life is an extraordinary inventory-risk advantage in food, and the anchovy exception shows where a premium seafood brand actually carries spoilage and cold-chain risk.

insights.claim: Fishwife insulated itself from the Moroccan ban by sourcing sardines from the Cornish fishery, which was the only MSC-certified sustainable sardine fishery in Europe when it started, and adding the Iberian fishery after it was MSC certified last year.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Sustainability certification doubled as supply-chain insurance here: sourcing from the best-regulated fisheries is what left the brand unimpaired when the largest fishery was closed to export.

insights.claim: Farmed salmon accounts for 70-80% of salmon eaten globally and is chosen by Fishwife largely for supply-chain reasons: it freezes and travels well, is harvested year round, and avoids the enormous lumpy cash outlay of seasonal wild purchasing.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Wild-caught sourcing is a working-capital decision as much as a quality one, which explains why aquaculture keeps taking share regardless of consumer preference messaging.
insights.quote: Farmed salmon makes up between 70 to 80% of the salmon that we're eating globally.

insights.claim: Farmed salmon prices are less volatile than wild salmon prices because year-round harvesting smooths the purchasing cycle, though farmed prices still fluctuate.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Input-cost predictability favors aquaculture-based products, a relevant edge for margin stability in any seafood-exposed packaged food name.

insights.claim: Attempting to stand up a wild Alaskan salmon supply chain failed because individual suppliers handled different salmon species that could not be mixed and the operation could not be scaled.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Fragmented, species-specific supply is a real barrier to scaling domestic wild seafood, which limits how fast any US wild-catch premium brand can grow.

themes.theme: Zero-to-one supply chain and scaling constraints

insights.claim: Fishwife's first year in 2021 ran on tiny US micro canneries in Oregon and Washington that serve sport fishermen and impose no minimum order quantity, which is how the brand bypassed the classic CPG cold-start problem of committing to huge first runs.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Micro-manufacturers with no MOQ are an underrated de-risking path for CPG launches versus the 50,000-unit first run typical of beverage; look for categories where such capacity still exists.

insights.claim: Fishwife's first Spanish cannery required roughly a 20,000-unit minimum order, and that single order of sardines with preserved lemon lasted the brand nearly a full year.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Sizing the true entry ticket for a category tells you how much capital a challenger needs before it has any demand signal; 20,000 units is trivially small versus most food manufacturing.
insights.quote: I think it was maybe 20,000 units

insights.claim: Demand planning was the hardest thing at Fishwife in year one, with two products out of stock for three months, yet brand building via press and influencer coverage still worked through the stockouts.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Early-stage brand equity can be built ahead of reliable supply, meaning stockouts in year one are a weaker negative signal for a consumer brand than they appear.

insights.claim: Fishwife executed a deliberate supply chain V2 transformation in 2023, targeting canneries capable of 80 to 100 million cans a year so the supply base could support essentially unlimited scale in the American market.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: The V1-to-V2 supply chain replatform is the operational inflection that separates a DTC novelty from a national retail brand; it is the milestone to underwrite in consumer diligence.
insights.quote: could produce 80 million cans a year, 100 million cans a year

insights.claim: Canned seafood is a long-lead industry where Fishwife must forecast to its canneries a year ahead, then six months, then three months before placing the PO so they can secure raw material, making forecast error the core operating risk for a high-growth brand.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: In long-lead categories, growth itself is the risk: exponential demand plus a 12-month planning horizon guarantees either stockouts or dead inventory.
insights.quote: we are trying to tell our canneries what we need a year ahead than six months ahead and three months ahead

insights.claim: There is a structural mismatch between Fishwife and its suppliers because multi-generational, non-venture-backed European family canneries consider 5% annual growth excellent and flat acceptable, while Fishwife's volume requests triple or quadruple year over year.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Supplier ambition, not supplier capacity, is often the true ceiling on a fast-growing consumer brand; diligence should test whether suppliers want to grow at all.
insights.quote: if they have 5% year over year growth, that's amazing. Flat fine.

insights.claim: European canneries agreed to work with an unknown American startup because establishing a brand in a foreign market is near impossible for them, and the US is an extremely attractive, high-paying market they could access without doing the marketing work themselves.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: A startup's real leverage with legacy manufacturers is offering market access they cannot build; that trade explains why supply-constrained categories can still open to new entrants.

insights.claim: European canneries in 2021 typically ran only one or two shifts a day, five days a week rather than three shifts seven days a week, and that idle capacity is what made entry possible without competing for line time.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Latent utilization in legacy manufacturing is a measurable entry window; once utilization normalizes, that window closes for the next entrant.

insights.claim: Current cannery-level scarcity for Fishwife comes from its own volume growth consuming far more canning line than either side forecast within two years, not from competing brands bidding for the same capacity.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: The constraint is self-inflicted scale rather than competitive crowding, which means capacity relief is a capex and partnership problem the company can actually solve.
insights.quote: we're taking up so much more canning line than we we thought we would be

themes.theme: Brand moat, pricing power and creator-economy costs

insights.claim: DTC is only about 20% of Fishwife's business and the company builds its economics around retail, because in food businesses retail is where the volume is.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: The DTC-native food brand that survives is the one that treats DTC as a marketing channel and retail as the P&L; channel mix is the diligence question.
insights.quote: food businesses you're going to build in, in retail like that is where the volume is

insights.claim: The 2010s DTC playbook of commodifying an expensive incumbent product and selling it cheaper via cheap Instagram ads no longer works, and the 2020s alternative is inventing a premium category that does not yet exist.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Rising paid-acquisition costs invert the DTC strategy from price disruption to category creation, changing which consumer businesses can earn a return on marketing spend.

insights.claim: Consumers were burned by DTC brands that claimed equal quality at lower cost, and the durable positioning now is genuinely high quality made by multi-generational European family canneries at a price that reflects it.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Provenance and verifiable craft, not cost disruption, is the defensible consumer story this cycle; brands whose story is only price face the credibility discount.

insights.claim: Consumer spending is highly concentrated, with roughly 50% of spending done by around 5% of the population, which is why a premium-priced product can support a whole company.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: K-shaped consumer concentration is the underlying reason premiumization keeps outperforming; target the affluent cohort rather than aggregate consumer sentiment.
insights.quote: like 50% of the spending right now is being done by like, I don't know, like 5%

insights.claim: Fishwife's moat is pricing power earned through five and a half years of online brand building in a category where that had never been done, and Millstein argues that brand-building work is very difficult to replicate even if the product is copied.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: In low-tech consumer categories the durable asset is narrative plus supply-chain agility, not the product formula; test whether an incumbent copycat can actually earn the same price.
insights.quote: that brand building work is very difficult to replicate

insights.claim: Despite the category clearly having heat, premium tinned fish has attracted fewer meaningful new entrants than most hot categories, which Millstein attributes to the difficulty of running a global seafood supply chain.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Operational difficulty is acting as the real barrier to entry here, so the incumbent's share may prove stickier than category-heat comparables would suggest.
insights.quote: less meaningful new entrants than many

insights.claim: Flat-fee influencer rates have become prohibitive for a mid-size CPG brand, with Fishwife quoted $30,000 to $40,000 for a single post from an account with around 800,000 followers.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Concrete creator-economy pricing: at these rates paid social is unaffordable for challenger food brands, pushing spend toward commission-based affiliate and product seeding.
insights.quote: I've been quoted, you know, $40,000, $30,000 for someone with, let's say like 800,000 followers, like we simply can't afford that.

insights.claim: Fishwife has done paid influencer collaborations fewer than ten times in its life, relying instead on a commission-based affiliate program and consistent product seeding, and reports no scarcity of aligned creators.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Pay-for-performance creator models can substitute for flat-fee media when the product itself is shareable, which materially changes CAC math for a premium consumer brand.

insights.claim: Brand collaborations at Fishwife involve no exchange of dollars and take months of joint product work, including a Whole Foods collaborative tote series developed over six months that Whole Foods had never done with any brand before.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Real collabs are unpaid distribution and credibility trades, not media buys, so they are a cheap growth lever that also signals genuine retailer commitment.
insights.quote: these collabs are so not pay to play in any way at all

insights.claim: The Fly By Jing chili crisp collaboration is structured as straightforward wholesale ingredient purchasing, with Fishwife buying the sauce at wholesale price and putting it in its product rather than any co-marketing payment.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Ingredient-level brand licensing at wholesale cost is a low-risk way to buy differentiation and borrowed audience without margin-destroying royalty structures.

insights.claim: Fishwife's hand-illustrated, colorful packaging was a deliberate counter-position against the white-and-blue, unbranded commodity look Americans associated with canned fish, with a staff illustrator producing artwork daily.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: In commodity categories, visual counter-positioning is the cheapest form of differentiation and directly underwrites the price premium.

insights.claim: A 15% tariff on European imports put in place in April 2025 costs Fishwife millions of dollars and directly hits gross margin on product imported from Spain and Portugal.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: A concrete, dollar-sized read on how EU tariffs flow through a food importer's P&L, useful for sizing margin risk in any European-sourced consumer goods business.
insights.quote: Europe has a 15%, tariff

insights.claim: Fishwife received a $1.5 million tariff refund in the prior month that showed up in its bank account, even as new tariffs were being applied.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Tariff refunds are materially cash-flow relevant for importers and create lumpy, non-operational swings in working capital that can distort quarterly reads.
insights.quote: We got refunded a million and a half dollars last month

insights.claim: A 35% import duty on tuna packed in olive oil has existed since Fishwife began importing that product, and because tariffs do not stack, the new tariff regime produced no incremental duty on that SKU.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Non-stacking of duties means pre-existing high-tariff SKUs can be insulated from new trade actions, an underappreciated nuance when modeling tariff exposure line by line.
insights.quote: there has been a 35% import duty on tuna packed in olive oil since we started importing that product

insights.claim: Aluminum tariffs have not meaningfully hit Fishwife because the canneries, not Fishwife, take ownership of the tins, though tin and aluminum prices have risen over its five years in business.
insights.speaker: Becca Millstein
insights.so_what: Where title to packaging sits in the supply chain determines who absorbs commodity tariffs; the same brand can be exposed to import duties yet insulated from metals tariffs.
